title: A&P: GI, Renal & Endocrine
summary: The plumbing and the chemistry: how food becomes fuel, how the kidney decides what stays in the blood, and how hormones hold glucose, salt and water in range. Built around the belly pain, the electrolyte panel and the diabetic emergency you will actually meet.

lessons.title: The GI tract, mouth to colon
lessons.body:
## One long tube, four jobs

Food is not inside you yet. The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is a tube roughly 9 meters long running from mouth to anus, and its inside (the lumen) is functionally outside the body. The tube has four jobs: break food into molecules small enough to cross the wall (digestion), move those molecules into blood or lymph (absorption), push contents along (motility), and dump the rest.

### Mouth and swallowing

Chewing increases surface area. Saliva adds amylase, which starts on starch. Swallowing (deglutition) has three phases: **oral** (voluntary, the tongue pushes the bolus back), **pharyngeal** (involuntary, the soft palate seals the nose, the epiglottis covers the larynx, and breathing stops for about `1 second`), and **esophageal** (peristalsis carries the bolus down in `5–10 seconds`).

> **Key:** The pharyngeal phase is where aspiration happens. Anything that blunts it — stroke, sedation, intoxication, dementia — sends food and secretions into the lungs instead of the stomach.

### Esophagus and its two gates

The esophagus is a muscular tube with a sphincter at each end. The upper esophageal sphincter keeps air out of the stomach. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) keeps acid in. When the LES leaks, acid burns the esophagus — gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) — which reads as burning chest pain after meals, worse lying flat.

> **Trap:** GERD and a heart attack feel the same to the patient. "It got better with antacids" does not rule out myocardial infarction.

### Stomach

The stomach holds about `1–1.5 L`, churns to mix, and secretes four things that matter:

- hydrochloric acid from parietal cells, pH `1.5–3.5`, which kills bacteria and activates enzymes
- pepsinogen from chief cells, which acid converts into pepsin, the protein-digesting enzyme
- intrinsic factor from parietal cells, required downstream to absorb vitamin B12
- a bicarbonate-rich mucus layer that stops acid from digesting the stomach itself

Strip that mucus layer — with Helicobacter pylori infection or chronic NSAIDs — and you get peptic ulcer disease.

### Small intestine: where absorption actually happens

About `6 m` long, lined with folds, villi and microvilli that give a surface area near `250 square meters`. Three parts, in order:

- **duodenum** (about `25 cm`): receives bile and pancreatic enzymes; absorbs iron, calcium and folate
- **jejunum** (about `2.5 m`): the workhorse — most carbohydrate, protein, fat and water-soluble vitamins
- **ileum** (about `3.5 m`): the only site that absorbs vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor, and the only site that recycles bile salts

### Colon and appendix

The large intestine reclaims water and electrolytes. About `1–1.5 L` of liquid chyme arrives daily and about `100–200 mL` leaves as stool. Its bacteria manufacture vitamin K. The appendix hangs off the cecum in the right lower quadrant; it holds lymphoid tissue and, when its narrow opening plugs, it becomes appendicitis.

> **On shift:** A patient who has lost colon length or has high-output diarrhea has lost that water-reclaiming step and dehydrates fast. Watch their orthostatics, not just their stool count.
keyPoints: The GI lumen is functionally outside the body — nothing counts until it crosses the wall.
The pharyngeal phase of swallowing protects the airway; lose it and you aspirate.
Acid plus pepsin digest food; the bicarbonate mucus layer is the only thing stopping them from digesting the stomach.
Absorption is a small-intestine job: iron/calcium/folate duodenum, most nutrients jejunum, B12 and bile salts ileum.
The colon's job is water: 1–1.5 L arrives, 100–200 mL leaves.

checks.q: Which segment absorbs vitamin B12?
checks.why: B12 must be bound to intrinsic factor from the stomach, and the receptors for that complex exist only in the terminal ileum. The duodenum handles iron, calcium and folate; the colon absorbs water.

checks.q: Which cell makes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
checks.why: Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor. Chief cells make pepsinogen. That pairing is why stomach disease causes B12 deficiency years later.

checks.q: Why does an intoxicated patient aspirate?
choices: Loss of the esophageal phase of swallowing
Loss of the voluntary oral phase only
Blunted pharyngeal phase, so the epiglottis and soft palate do not seal
checks.why: The pharyngeal phase is the involuntary reflex that closes the airway during a swallow. Sedation blunts it. The oral phase is voluntary and the esophageal phase happens after the airway is already past.

lessons.title: Liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen
lessons.body:
## The organs that feed the tube

Four organs sit alongside the GI tract and do chemistry the tube cannot.

### The liver: factory and filter

The liver fills the right upper quadrant under the diaphragm, weighs about `1.5 kg`, and gets roughly `75%` of its blood from the portal vein — blood that already passed through the intestines. Everything absorbed goes through the liver before it reaches the rest of you (first-pass metabolism). Its jobs:

- **Bile**: `500–1000 mL/day`, which emulsifies fat so lipase can work
- **Clotting factors**: nearly all of them (II, V, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen)
- **Albumin**: about `10–15 g/day`, the protein that holds fluid inside vessels (oncotic pressure)
- **Glucose storage**: stores glycogen, releases glucose between meals
- **Drug metabolism**: the cytochrome P450 enzymes
- **Ammonia to urea**: converts the nitrogen waste of protein breakdown into urea the kidney can excrete
- **Bilirubin**: takes the pigment from broken red cells and conjugates it into bile

### Liver failure is that list read backwards

Every sign maps to a lost job.

- No bilirubin handling means **jaundice** — yellow sclera appear around a total bilirubin of `2.5–3 mg/dL`.
- No albumin means fluid leaves the vessels: **ascites** and peripheral edema.
- No clotting factors means **coagulopathy** — a rising INR, easy bruising, and bleeding that will not stop.
- No ammonia clearance means **hepatic encephalopathy**: confusion, asterixis (the flapping hand tremor), then coma.
- A scarred liver resists portal blood flow, so pressure backs up: **portal hypertension**, esophageal varices, an enlarged spleen, and dilated abdominal wall veins.

> **Key:** A cirrhotic patient with a GI bleed is bleeding from high-pressure varices with no clotting factors to stop it. That is two lethal problems at once.

### Gallbladder and the biliary tree

The gallbladder stores and concentrates `30–50 mL` of bile. Fat arriving in the duodenum releases cholecystokinin (CCK), which squeezes it. Bile leaves by the cystic duct, joins the common hepatic duct to become the common bile duct, and enters the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater.

A stone stuck in the cystic duct inflames the gallbladder: **cholecystitis**. A stone in the common bile duct backs bile into the blood — pain plus jaundice plus fever is **ascending cholangitis**, a surgical emergency. The same stone can block the pancreatic outlet and cause **gallstone pancreatitis**.

### Pancreas: two organs sharing a building

- **Exocrine** (about `99%` of the tissue): `1–1.5 L/day` of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice. Amylase for starch, lipase for fat, trypsin and chymotrypsin for protein. Enzymes leave inactive and are switched on in the duodenum. If they activate early, the pancreas digests itself — pancreatitis, most often from gallstones or alcohol.
- **Endocrine** (the islets of Langerhans, about `1%`): beta cells make insulin, alpha cells make glucagon, delta cells make somatostatin.

### Spleen

Left upper quadrant, tucked behind ribs `9–11`. It filters aging red cells and is a major factory for antibodies against encapsulated bacteria. It is the organ most often injured in blunt abdominal trauma, and blood pooling under the left diaphragm refers pain to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign).

> **On shift:** Ask an asplenic patient about vaccines and fever plans. Without a spleen, pneumococcus can go from cough to septic shock in hours.
keyPoints: Portal blood means everything absorbed hits the liver first — that is first-pass metabolism.
Every liver failure sign is one lost liver job: jaundice, ascites, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, portal hypertension.
Pain plus jaundice plus fever is ascending cholangitis, not simple biliary colic.
Pancreatic enzymes are shipped inactive; early activation is pancreatitis.
The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma and refers pain to the left shoulder.

checks.q: A cirrhotic patient has an INR of 2.4 and is not on any anticoagulant. Why?
choices: The liver cannot make clotting factors
Platelets are being destroyed in the marrow
checks.why: The liver synthesizes nearly every clotting factor, so failure raises the INR directly. Splenic sequestration does lower platelets in cirrhosis, but that is a separate problem and does not change the INR.

checks.q: Which liver function explains ascites?
checks.why: Albumin holds fluid inside vessels by oncotic pressure. Without it, fluid leaks into the peritoneal cavity. Portal hypertension adds to it, but the missing protein is the reason it keeps reaccumulating.

lessons.title: Abdominal geography and the pain map
lessons.body:
## Divide the belly before you touch it

### Four quadrants

Draw a cross through the umbilicus.

| Quadrant | What lives there | Classic problem |
|---|---|---|
| Right upper | liver, gallbladder, duodenum, pancreas head, right kidney | cholecystitis, hepatitis |
| Left upper | stomach, spleen, pancreas tail, left kidney | splenic injury, gastritis |
| Right lower | appendix, cecum, right ovary and tube, right ureter | appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy |
| Left lower | sigmoid colon, left ovary and tube, left ureter | diverticulitis, ovarian torsion |

### Nine regions

Two vertical midclavicular lines and two horizontal lines carve nine boxes: right hypochondriac, **epigastric**, left hypochondriac across the top; right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar in the middle; right iliac, **hypogastric** (suprapubic), left iliac at the bottom.

Epigastric pain is the one that must never be filed under "indigestion": pancreatitis, peptic ulcer and inferior wall myocardial infarction all present there. Suprapubic points at bladder or uterus. Flank points at kidney.

### Visceral versus parietal pain

Hollow organs carry sparse unmyelinated nerves that report to the spinal segment the organ grew from, not where it ended up. So **visceral pain** is dull, crampy, poorly localized, usually midline, and comes with nausea and sweating. The patient cannot point to it with one finger.

The **parietal peritoneum** lining the abdominal wall is somatic tissue with precise mapping. When inflammation reaches it, pain turns sharp, constant and localized.

That is appendicitis in one sentence. The inflamed appendix first reports as vague periumbilical pain at the T10 level. Over `12–24 hours` the inflammation touches the parietal peritoneum above it, and the pain sharpens and migrates to **McBurney's point**, one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine toward the umbilicus.

> **Key:** Pain that starts vague and central and becomes sharp and focal is inflammation reaching the peritoneum. The migration is the finding, not a detail.

### Referred pain worth memorizing

| Source | Refers to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Diaphragm, spleen, free blood | left shoulder, called Kehr's sign | phrenic nerve, C3–C5 |
| Gallbladder | right shoulder or scapula | shared phrenic and somatic segments |
| Pancreas | straight through to the back | retroperitoneal position |
| Ureteral stone | flank down to the groin, colicky | shared T10–L1 segments |
| Inferior wall heart attack | epigastrium, jaw, left arm | shared T1–T4 input |

### Signs that go with the spots

- **Murphy's sign**: press under the right costal margin and ask for a deep breath; the patient stops mid-breath — cholecystitis.
- **McBurney's point tenderness** and **Rovsing's sign** (pressing the left lower quadrant hurts the right) — appendicitis.
- **Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness**: a thump over the flank hurts — pyelonephritis, not simple cystitis.
- **Grey Turner and Cullen signs**: flank or periumbilical bruising from retroperitoneal bleeding, late and uncommon.

> **On the exam:** They give you the migration, the point and the timeline and expect the diagnosis with no imaging and no labs. Learn the story, not just the location.
keyPoints: Four quadrants for speed, nine regions for precision; epigastric pain includes the heart.
Visceral pain is dull, midline and unlocalizable; parietal pain is sharp, constant and pointable.
Appendicitis pain migrates from periumbilical to McBurney's point as the peritoneum gets involved.
Kehr's sign is left shoulder pain from blood or air under the diaphragm via the phrenic nerve.
CVA tenderness is what separates pyelonephritis from a bladder infection.

checks.q: A 20-year-old had vague pain around the navel yesterday; today it is sharp and fixed in the right lower quadrant. What happened?
choices: The pain is referred from the gallbladder
Inflammation spread to the parietal peritoneum over the appendix
The appendix ruptured and pain should now be diffuse
checks.why: Migration from vague periumbilical visceral pain to sharp localized parietal pain is the classic appendicitis timeline. Rupture typically brings diffuse peritonitis and a sicker patient, not a single focal point.

checks.q: A trauma patient complains of left shoulder pain with no shoulder injury. What should you suspect?
choices: Blood irritating the left diaphragm from a splenic injury
checks.why: That is Kehr's sign. The phrenic nerve carries diaphragmatic irritation to C3–C5 dermatomes at the shoulder. The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma.

checks.q: Which finding points to the gallbladder?
checks.why: Murphy's sign is inspiratory arrest on right upper quadrant palpation. Rovsing and McBurney are appendicitis findings; CVA tenderness points at the kidney.

lessons.title: The acute abdomen: peritonitis, obstruction, bleeding
lessons.body:
## Three patterns that put a belly on the surgery board

### Peritonitis

The peritoneum is a two-layer sac holding about `50 mL` of lubricating fluid. Spill anything irritating into that space — acid from a perforated ulcer, stool from a ruptured diverticulum, blood, pus, bile — and the parietal layer inflames. You get:

- **guarding**: abdominal wall muscles tighten, first voluntarily, then involuntarily
- **rigidity**: a board-like belly, involuntary and late
- **rebound tenderness**: worse on release than on pressure
- **silence**: bowel sounds disappear as the gut stops (ileus)

Posture sorts the diagnosis. **Peritonitis patients lie perfectly still**, because any motion drags inflamed surfaces across each other. **Colic patients writhe** — kidney stone, early obstruction — because nothing relieves a squeezing hollow organ.

> **Key:** Still and rigid means peritoneum. Restless and unable to get comfortable means a hollow organ squeezing.

### Bowel obstruction

Something blocks the tube. Gas, secretions and food pile up behind it, the bowel distends, the wall swells, blood flow drops, and fluid pours into the lumen instead of back into the blood. That is **third spacing**: the patient is volume-depleted before anything has left the body.

Causes in order: adhesions from prior surgery (about `60%` of small bowel obstructions), hernias, then tumors. In the large bowel it is cancer, volvulus, or diverticular stricture.

| | Small bowel | Large bowel |
|---|---|---|
| Vomiting | early, bilious | late, feculent |
| Distension | moderate | marked |
| Cramping interval | every `3–5 min` | every `10–15 min` |
| No stool or gas (obstipation) | later | early |

Bowel sounds are high-pitched and tinkling early, absent late. The feared turn is **strangulation**: blood supply cut off, cramping pain becomes constant, fever and tachycardia appear, lactate rises, and bowel dies within hours.

### GI bleeding: above or below the ligament of Treitz

That ligament at the duodenojejunal junction is the dividing line.

**Upper GI bleed** (esophagus, stomach, duodenum): **hematemesis**, bright red vomited blood, or **coffee-ground emesis**, blood that acid has denatured. Blood moving down the tract becomes **melena** — black, tarry, foul stool — which needs about `14 hours` and as little as `50 mL` of blood. Causes: peptic ulcer (most common), esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastritis.

**Lower GI bleed** (below Treitz): **hematochezia**, bright red or maroon blood per rectum. Causes: diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, colitis, cancer.

> **Trap:** A brisk upper bleed can look like hematochezia because blood moves too fast to turn black. Bright red rectal bleeding with shock is an upper bleed until proven otherwise.

The lab clue: in an upper bleed, blood protein is digested and absorbed as nitrogen, so **BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine**. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above `30:1` points upstairs. Hemoglobin lags behind reality — a patient losing whole blood has not yet diluted, so an initial hemoglobin of `13 g/dL` does not mean they are not hemorrhaging.

> **On shift:** Varices bleed hard and painlessly; ulcers usually hurt first. Both get two large-bore IVs, a type and screen, and someone watching the airway, because vomiting blood plus altered mental status is an intubation waiting to happen.
keyPoints: Guarding, rigidity and rebound with a motionless patient means peritoneal inflammation.
Adhesions cause about 60% of small bowel obstructions; third spacing depletes volume before any vomiting.
Strangulation announces itself when crampy pain becomes constant and fever and tachycardia appear.
The ligament of Treitz splits upper from lower GI bleeding; melena needs about 50 mL of blood and 14 hours.
A BUN:creatinine ratio above 30:1 with a GI bleed points to an upper source.

checks.q: A patient with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting has had no surgery and a tender bulge in the groin. Most likely cause of the obstruction?
checks.why: Adhesions are the top cause overall, but they require prior surgery. With no surgical history and a groin bulge, an incarcerated hernia is the obstruction. Cancer and volvulus are large bowel causes and present with late vomiting.

checks.q: Black tarry stool with a BUN of 52 and a creatinine of 1.1 suggests bleeding from where?
checks.why: Melena plus a BUN:creatinine ratio near 47:1 is an upper source. Digested blood protein raises BUN. Colonic and anorectal bleeding arrives as bright red or maroon blood and does not raise the BUN that way.

lessons.title: The kidney and the nephron
lessons.body:
## Two organs that decide what stays in the blood

Each kidney is about `11 cm` long, sits behind the peritoneum at the T12–L3 level, and holds roughly `1 million` nephrons. Together they take `20–25%` of cardiac output, about `1.2 L of blood per minute`.

Six jobs: clear nitrogen waste, balance water, balance electrolytes, manage acid-base, regulate blood pressure through renin, and make erythropoietin while activating vitamin D.

### The nephron, one station at a time

**1. Glomerulus — filtration.** A capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule. Pressure pushes plasma through a filter that keeps cells and large proteins behind. Normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about `100–125 mL/min`, which is roughly `180 L` filtered per day. You urinate `1–2 L`, so more than `99%` of that is reclaimed downstream. Protein or blood in urine means the filter itself is damaged.

**2. Proximal convoluted tubule — bulk reabsorption.** About `65%` of sodium and water return here, along with essentially all glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. Glucose transport saturates near a serum glucose of `180 mg/dL` — which is exactly why diabetics spill sugar into urine and drag water out with it.

**3. Loop of Henle — the concentrator.** The descending limb lets water out but not salt. The thick ascending limb pumps sodium, potassium and chloride out but is waterproof. The result is a salty medulla, and that gradient is the machinery that lets you make concentrated urine at all.

**4. Distal convoluted tubule — fine tuning.** Sodium and chloride reabsorption, plus calcium under parathyroid hormone control.

**5. Collecting duct — the hormone floor.**

- **Aldosterone**, from the adrenal cortex, reabsorbs sodium and secretes potassium. Save salt, dump potassium.
- **Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)**, from the posterior pituitary, inserts water channels. ADH present means water comes back and urine concentrates.

### Where the diuretics act

| Class | Site | Effect on potassium |
|---|---|---|
| Loop: furosemide, bumetanide | thick ascending limb | lowers it |
| Thiazide: hydrochlorothiazide | distal convoluted tubule | lowers it |
| Potassium-sparing: spironolactone, triamterene | collecting duct | raises it |
| Carbonic anhydrase: acetazolamide | proximal tubule | mild loss |

Loops are the strongest because they block the largest sodium pump and destroy the concentrating gradient at the same time. They lower potassium twice over: more sodium arrives at the collecting duct to be traded for potassium, and volume loss raises aldosterone, which does the same thing. That is why a patient on furosemide gets a potassium checked and usually supplemented.

> **Key:** Every diuretic question is answered by naming the segment. Name the segment and the electrolyte consequence follows.

> **Trap:** Spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor plus a potassium supplement in a patient with a weak kidney is a recipe for lethal hyperkalemia — and that exact combination appears on real medication lists constantly.

### Renin and blood pressure

Low renal perfusion makes juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin makes angiotensin I, angiotensin-converting enzyme (mostly in the lung) makes angiotensin II, and angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that also triggers aldosterone and ADH. ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril and ARBs such as losartan block this loop, which is why they lower blood pressure, protect diabetic kidneys, and raise potassium.
keyPoints: Normal GFR is about 100–125 mL/min, roughly 180 L filtered daily to make 1–2 L of urine.
Proximal tubule does bulk reabsorption; glucose spills above a serum glucose near 180 mg/dL.
The loop of Henle builds the salty medulla that makes concentrated urine possible.
Aldosterone saves sodium and dumps potassium; ADH saves water.
Name the tubule segment a diuretic blocks and its potassium effect follows automatically.

checks.q: Furosemide acts on which part of the nephron?
choices: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
checks.why: Loop diuretics block the sodium-potassium-chloride transporter in the thick ascending limb. Thiazides work at the distal tubule and potassium-sparing agents at the collecting duct.

checks.q: Which agent raises serum potassium?
checks.why: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the collecting duct, so sodium is lost and potassium is kept. Loops and thiazides both drive potassium down; acetazolamide causes only mild loss.

checks.q: Why does a diabetic with a glucose of 400 mg/dL urinate constantly?
choices: Glucose exceeds the proximal tubule transport maximum, stays in the filtrate, and pulls water with it
The glomerular filter is damaged by sugar within hours
checks.why: Proximal glucose reabsorption saturates around 180 mg/dL. Unreabsorbed glucose is an osmotic load that holds water in the tubule — an osmotic diuresis. ADH and aldosterone are not the primary driver here.

lessons.title: Fluids: compartments, osmolality, and what you hang
lessons.body:
## Water is not one pool

Total body water is about `60%` of body weight in an average adult male, about `50%` in a female, up to `75%` in a newborn, and lower in the elderly and in obesity because fat holds little water. A `70 kg` man carries roughly `42 L`.

Split it:

- **Intracellular fluid (ICF)** — two thirds, about `28 L`. The dominant cation inside cells is **potassium**.
- **Extracellular fluid (ECF)** — one third, about `14 L`, divided into interstitial fluid (about `11 L`, between cells) and plasma (about `3 L`, inside vessels). The dominant cation outside cells is **sodium**.

### Osmolality is the rule that moves water

Water follows solute. Serum osmolality normally runs `275–295 mOsm/kg`, and you can estimate it as `2 x Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8`. Sodium dominates that equation, which gives you the single most useful fact in fluid physiology: **sodium concentration is a water problem, not a salt problem**. A low sodium usually means too much water for the salt present, not too little salt.

Two sensors defend osmolality. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger thirst, and they trigger ADH release so the kidney keeps water. A rise of only `1–2%` switches both on.

> **Key:** Sodium tells you about water. Volume status — blood pressure, heart rate, skin turgor, urine output, jugular veins — tells you about salt and volume. They are two separate questions and you must ask both.

### Dehydration versus volume depletion versus third spacing

**Dehydration** is losing water alone: osmolality and sodium rise, the patient is thirsty, urine is concentrated and scant. **Volume depletion** is losing salt and water together — hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea, burns — so the vessels empty while the sodium may read perfectly normal. **Third spacing** is fluid still inside the body but not inside the vessels: bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, burns, ascites. That patient can gain `4 kg` and still be in shock.

### The three bags you will hang

| Fluid | Tonicity | Where it ends up |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9% normal saline, `154 mEq/L` sodium and chloride | isotonic | stays in the ECF; only about one quarter remains intravascular |
| Lactated Ringer's: `130` Na, `4` K, `3` Ca, `109` Cl, `28` lactate | isotonic | same distribution, plus lactate the liver turns into bicarbonate |
| 5% dextrose in water | isotonic in the bag, hypotonic in the body | dextrose is burned, the free water spreads everywhere; only about one twelfth stays intravascular |

That table answers the classic question: give D5W to a hemorrhaging patient and almost none of it stays where you need it. Large-volume normal saline can produce a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, which is why balanced solutions such as lactated Ringer's are preferred in many resuscitation protocols — but the choice varies by protocol.

Hypertonic `3%` saline is a targeted drug for symptomatic hyponatremia or raised intracranial pressure, not a resuscitation fluid.

> **On shift:** Urine output is the cheapest continuous readout of perfusion you have. `0.5 mL/kg/hr` in an adult and `1 mL/kg/hr` in a child is the floor.
keyPoints: Total body water is about 60% of weight: two thirds intracellular, one third extracellular, and only about 3 L is plasma.
Potassium rules inside cells, sodium rules outside; osmolality of 275–295 mOsm/kg is the set point.
Serum sodium answers a water question; blood pressure and urine output answer the volume question.
Third-spaced patients gain weight and are still intravascularly dry.
Only about one quarter of normal saline and one twelfth of D5W stays in the vessels.

checks.q: Why is D5W a poor choice for a hemorrhaging patient?
choices: It is hypertonic and pulls water out of cells
Once the dextrose is metabolized it behaves as free water and spreads through every compartment
checks.why: D5W is isotonic only in the bag. After the sugar is burned, what remains is free water, and roughly one twelfth stays intravascular. Hyperchloremic acidosis is a normal saline problem, not a D5W problem.

checks.q: A pancreatitis patient has gained 4 kg since admission but is tachycardic with a blood pressure of 88/52. What is happening?
choices: Fluid has third-spaced out of the vessels, so they are intravascularly depleted despite the weight gain
The weight gain is a scale error
checks.why: Pancreatitis drives huge third spacing into the retroperitoneum and gut. The fluid is inside the body but not in the vessels. Diuresing this patient would make the shock worse.

lessons.title: Electrolytes that kill
lessons.body:
## Five numbers and the trouble each one causes

### Sodium, normal `135–145 mEq/L`

Sodium sets extracellular osmolality, so sodium sets brain cell volume.

**Hyponatremia** lets water move into brain cells and swell them. Below `125` expect headache, nausea and confusion; below `120`, or after any rapid drop, expect seizures. Causes: SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis, thiazide diuretics, excess free water intake, adrenal insufficiency.

Correct it **slowly**. Raising sodium faster than `8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours` risks osmotic demyelination, a permanent brainstem injury. The one exception is an actively seizing patient, who gets small boluses of `3%` hypertonic saline to buy a few points fast.

**Hypernatremia** above `145` is nearly always water loss: fever, diabetes insipidus, or simply no access to water. Thirst, lethargy, irritability, seizures. It also corrects slowly, because rehydrating a brain too fast causes cerebral edema.

### Potassium, normal `3.5–5.0 mEq/L`

Only about `2%` of body potassium is in blood; the rest is inside cells. The ratio across the cell membrane sets the resting membrane potential — which is why potassium is the electrolyte that stops hearts.

Hyperkalemia causes: renal failure and missed dialysis (the big one), ACE inhibitors and ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, crush injury and rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, acidosis (hydrogen moves into cells and potassium moves out), and a hemolyzed blood sample that fooled everyone.

The ECG climbs a predictable ladder:

1. peaked, narrow, tented T waves, around `5.5–6.5`
2. flattened P waves and a long PR interval, around `6.5–7.5`
3. widened QRS, around `7–8`
4. sine wave, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole, above `8`

Treatment order, and the reason for it:

1. **Calcium gluconate `1 g` IV** (or calcium chloride `1 g` through a central line) stabilizes the cardiac membrane within `1–3 minutes`. It lowers nothing. It buys time.
2. **Shift it into cells**: regular insulin `10 units` IV with `25 g` dextrose, onset about `15 minutes`, lasting `4–6 hours`; albuterol `10–20 mg` nebulized; sodium bicarbonate if the patient is acidotic.
3. **Remove it**: a loop diuretic if the kidneys still make urine, oral potassium binders, and **dialysis**, which is the only definitive answer in renal failure.

> **Key:** Calcium protects, insulin and albuterol move, only diuresis and dialysis remove. Steps one and two are temporary — that potassium is coming back out of the cells.

**Hypokalemia** below `3.5` brings weakness, cramps, ileus, flattened T waves, prominent U waves and ventricular arrhythmias. Diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea and insulin are the usual causes. You cannot fix stubborn hypokalemia without also replacing magnesium.

### Calcium, total `8.5–10.5 mg/dL`, ionized `4.6–5.3 mg/dL`

Only the ionized fraction is biologically active. About `40%` of calcium rides on albumin, so a low-albumin patient shows a falsely low total. Correct it by adding `0.8 mg/dL` to the calcium for every `1 g/dL` the albumin sits below `4 g/dL`.

- **Hypocalcemia**: tingling around the mouth and fingertips, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, tetany, a prolonged QT, laryngospasm.
- **Hypercalcemia**: stones, bones, groans and psychiatric overtones — kidney stones, bone pain, constipation, confusion — with a shortened QT.

### Magnesium, normal `1.5–2.5 mg/dL`

Low magnesium causes **torsades de pointes**, the twisting polymorphic ventricular tachycardia treated with magnesium sulfate `1–2 g` IV. It also makes potassium impossible to correct, and it is nearly universal in alcohol use disorder.

### Phosphate, normal `2.5–4.5 mg/dL`

It moves opposite calcium. It climbs in renal failure and falls during refeeding and during DKA treatment, where severe hypophosphatemia can weaken the diaphragm.

### The kidney's acid-base job in one paragraph

Lungs handle acid in minutes by blowing off carbon dioxide. Kidneys handle it over hours to days: they reabsorb filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule, generate new bicarbonate, and excrete hydrogen buffered as ammonium and phosphate. Lose the kidneys and you get a wide anion gap metabolic acidosis — the classic missed-dialysis picture, sitting right alongside the hyperkalemia.
keyPoints: Sodium 135–145; correct hyponatremia no faster than 8–10 mEq/L per day or risk osmotic demyelination.
Potassium 3.5–5.0; the ECG ladder is peaked T waves, then flat P and long PR, then wide QRS, then sine wave.
Hyperkalemia order: calcium protects, insulin and albuterol shift, diuresis and dialysis remove.
Only ionized calcium matters; add 0.8 mg/dL per 1 g/dL the albumin is below 4.
Magnesium 1.5–2.5; low magnesium causes torsades and blocks potassium repletion.

checks.q: A dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.6 and a QRS of 150 ms. What is given first?
checks.why: Calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane in 1–3 minutes and prevents arrest while everything else is arranged. Insulin and albuterol shift potassium but take 15–30 minutes, and dialysis takes far longer to set up.

checks.q: A patient has a total calcium of 7.6 mg/dL and an albumin of 2.0 g/dL. What is the corrected calcium?
choices: Calcium cannot be corrected for albumin
checks.why: Albumin is 2 g/dL below 4, so add 0.8 twice: 7.6 plus 1.6 equals about 9.2. Treating this patient for hypocalcemia based on the uncorrected number would be wrong.

checks.q: Why does magnesium matter when potassium will not come up?
choices: Low magnesium promotes renal potassium wasting, so repletion fails until magnesium is corrected
checks.why: Hypomagnesemia opens renal potassium channels and the kidney dumps what you give. Replace magnesium and the potassium finally holds. Magnesium is not converted into potassium and does not interfere with the assay.

lessons.title: Kidney failure, dialysis, and the urinary tract
lessons.body:
## When filtration stops

### Acute kidney injury (AKI)

Defined by a creatinine rise of `0.3 mg/dL` in 48 hours, a `50%` rise within 7 days, or urine output under `0.5 mL/kg/hr` for 6 hours. Three categories, and the category is the treatment.

**Pre-renal**, about `60–70%` of cases. The kidney is fine; blood is not reaching it. Hypovolemia, hemorrhage, heart failure, sepsis, and drugs that cripple glomerular autoregulation such as NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. The kidney responds correctly by hoarding sodium and urea, so the **BUN-to-creatinine ratio climbs above `20:1`**, urine is concentrated, and urine sodium is low. Fluid fixes it.

**Intrinsic**. The kidney tissue itself is damaged, most often acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from prolonged ischemia or from toxins — contrast, aminoglycosides, myoglobin released by rhabdomyolysis. Damaged tubules can no longer concentrate or hoard, so the **ratio falls back to about `10–15:1`**, urine sodium rises, and muddy brown granular casts appear. Fluid will not revive dead tubules.

**Post-renal**. The plumbing is blocked: prostate enlargement, a stone in a single functioning kidney, tumor, or a clotted urinary catheter. A bladder scan and a catheter can reverse it in minutes.

> **On shift:** Post-renal is the fastest to fix and the most often missed. Any patient who has stopped making urine gets a bladder scan before anyone argues about fluids.

### Chronic kidney disease, staged by GFR

| Stage | GFR in `mL/min/1.73 m2` |
|---|---|
| 1 | `90` or above with evidence of kidney damage |
| 2 | `60–89` |
| 3a and 3b | `45–59` and `30–44` |
| 4 | `15–29` |
| 5, end stage | under `15`, or on dialysis |

Chronic kidney disease drags along anemia (no erythropoietin), bone disease (no activated vitamin D, high phosphate, high parathyroid hormone), metabolic acidosis, hypertension, and a potassium with nowhere to go.

### Dialysis

**Hemodialysis** pumps blood past a membrane against dialysate, typically `3–4 hours`, three days a week. Access, in order of preference: an arteriovenous **fistula** (artery sewn to vein, needs `2–3 months` to mature, lowest infection rate), a **graft** (synthetic, usable in `2–3 weeks`), or a **tunneled catheter** (usable immediately, highest infection risk). Feel a fistula for a thrill; listen for a bruit.

> **Trap:** Nothing goes in the access arm. No blood pressure cuff, no IV, no blood draw, no tourniquet. Clotting that fistula sends the patient to the operating room.

**Peritoneal dialysis** uses the patient's own peritoneum as the membrane, with fluid dwelling in the abdomen. Its emergency is peritonitis: cloudy drainage plus abdominal pain.

**The missed-dialysis emergency is two problems stacked**: hyperkalemia that can arrest the heart, and volume overload that floods the lungs. A dialysis patient who skipped a session and now feels weak or short of breath gets an ECG immediately, not after the labs come back.

### The urinary tract

Ureters run about `25 cm` and narrow at three points — the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction — which is exactly where stones lodge.

- **Cystitis**: burning, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, **no fever**. Mostly E. coli, mostly women, because the female urethra is about `4 cm` against roughly `20 cm` in men.
- **Pyelonephritis**: the infection climbed. Fever, chills, flank pain and **CVA tenderness**. That single finding moves the patient from oral antibiotics at home to IV antibiotics and possible admission.
- **Nephrolithiasis**: sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, and a patient who cannot lie still. Most stones under `5 mm` pass on their own.
- **Urinary retention**: usually benign prostatic hyperplasia in older men, or anticholinergic drugs. A tender distended suprapubic bladder; a catheter can drain over a liter.
- **Hematuria**: infection, stone, trauma or cancer until proven otherwise. Painless gross hematuria in a smoker over 50 is bladder cancer until the workup says otherwise.
keyPoints: AKI is pre-renal, intrinsic or post-renal; the category dictates whether fluid, time or a catheter is the fix.
A BUN:creatinine ratio above 20:1 with concentrated urine says pre-renal; about 10–15:1 with muddy brown casts says ATN.
CKD stage 5 is a GFR under 15 or dialysis dependence, and brings anemia, bone disease and acidosis.
Nothing goes in the dialysis access arm — no cuff, no IV, no draw.
Missed dialysis equals hyperkalemia plus pulmonary edema; get the ECG first.

checks.q: A hypotensive patient has a BUN of 64, a creatinine of 1.6 and a urine sodium of 12 mEq/L. Which AKI category?
checks.why: A ratio of 40:1 with avid sodium retention means the tubules still work and are hoarding — pre-renal. ATN loses that ability and shows urine sodium above 40 with muddy brown casts. Obstruction is diagnosed by bladder scan and imaging.

checks.q: Which finding separates pyelonephritis from simple cystitis?
checks.why: Burning, frequency and cloudy urine occur in both. Fever plus CVA tenderness means the infection has reached the kidney, which changes the antibiotic route and the disposition.

lessons.title: Hormones, the pituitary, and the glands
lessons.body:
## Chemical messages and the thermostat that controls them

A hormone is a molecule released into blood by one tissue that changes the behavior of a distant tissue carrying the matching receptor. Nerves are fast and local; hormones are slower and body-wide.

Almost every endocrine system is a **negative feedback loop**, exactly like a thermostat. The hypothalamus releases a releasing hormone, the anterior pituitary releases a stimulating hormone, the target gland releases the final hormone, and that final hormone shuts the first two off.

> **Key:** Low target hormone with a high stimulating hormone means the gland is failing and the pituitary is shouting at it. High target hormone with a low stimulating hormone means the gland is running on its own.

### The axes in plain words

| Hypothalamus | Anterior pituitary | Target | Final hormone |
|---|---|---|---|
| TRH | TSH | thyroid | T4 and T3 |
| CRH | ACTH | adrenal cortex | cortisol |
| GHRH | growth hormone | liver and tissues | IGF-1 |
| dopamine, which inhibits | prolactin | breast | milk |

The **posterior pituitary** manufactures nothing. It stores and releases two hormones made in the hypothalamus: **ADH**, which controls water, and **oxytocin**, which contracts the uterus and lets milk down.

### Thyroid: the metabolic gas pedal

The thyroid wraps the trachea and builds T4 and T3 from iodine. Everything in the body speeds up or slows down with it, so the two diseases read as mirror images.

| Hyperthyroid, usually Graves disease | Hypothyroid, usually Hashimoto thyroiditis |
|---|---|
| weight loss, heat intolerance | weight gain, cold intolerance |
| tachycardia, atrial fibrillation | bradycardia |
| anxiety, tremor, diarrhea | depression, slowed thought, constipation |
| warm moist skin, bulging eyes | dry coarse skin, hair loss |

The emergencies are the extremes. **Thyroid storm**: temperature above `40 C`, heart rate over `140`, agitation or delirium, usually triggered by infection, surgery or trauma. **Myxedema coma**: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention, hyponatremia and depressed consciousness, typically an elderly patient in winter.

### Adrenals: cortex outside, medulla inside

The cortex makes salt, sugar and sex hormones: **aldosterone** (holds sodium and water, dumps potassium), **cortisol** (raises glucose, suppresses inflammation and immunity, supports vascular tone under stress), and androgens. The medulla makes **catecholamines** — epinephrine and norepinephrine.

**Adrenal crisis** is the one that kills. A patient on chronic steroids has a suppressed axis; their own adrenals have gone quiet. Stop the steroid abruptly, or hit them with surgery, infection or trauma without extra steroid, and they crash: hypotension that does not answer fluids or pressors, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, vomiting and abdominal pain. Treatment is hydrocortisone `100 mg IV` with fluids and glucose.

> **Trap:** Anyone who has taken prednisone for more than about three weeks in the past year is steroid-dependent until proven otherwise. Ask the question before the pressure drops, not after.

**Pheochromocytoma** is a catecholamine-secreting tumor: episodic severe hypertension with headache, palpitations and drenching sweats.

### Calcium: parathyroid hormone and vitamin D

Parathyroid hormone from four small glands behind the thyroid raises calcium three ways: it pulls calcium from bone, reabsorbs it in the distal tubule, and activates vitamin D in the kidney so the gut absorbs more. It lowers phosphate. Calcitonin from the thyroid does the reverse and matters little in adults. Neck surgery that removes the parathyroids produces hypocalcemia and tetany within `24–48 hours`.

### The ADH mirror image

| | SIADH | Diabetes insipidus |
|---|---|---|
| ADH | too much | too little, or kidney ignores it |
| Urine | concentrated, low volume | dilute, `3–20 L/day` |
| Serum sodium | low | high |
| Treatment | fluid restriction | desmopressin and free water |

### Pregnancy hormones, briefly

hCG from the implanting placenta is detectable in blood about `8–11 days` after conception and doubles roughly every `48 hours` early on; that is what a pregnancy test measures. Progesterone maintains the uterine lining and relaxes smooth muscle everywhere, which is why pregnancy brings reflux, constipation and urinary stasis. An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus can build antibodies against it, which is why RhoGAM is given after bleeding events and at about `28 weeks`.
keyPoints: Read any axis by pairing the stimulating hormone with the final hormone: high TSH with low T4 means the gland failed.
The posterior pituitary only stores ADH and oxytocin; the hypothalamus makes them.
Hyper and hypothyroid signs are mirror images; the emergencies are thyroid storm and myxedema coma.
Adrenal crisis is refractory hypotension with low glucose, low sodium and high potassium — give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV.
SIADH is too much ADH with a low sodium; diabetes insipidus is too little with a high sodium and huge urine output.

checks.q: A patient has a TSH of 18 and a free T4 below the reference range. What does that mean?
choices: Primary hypothyroidism — the gland is failing and the pituitary is pushing harder
checks.why: A high stimulating hormone with a low final hormone localizes the failure to the target gland. Pituitary failure would show a low or inappropriately normal TSH with a low T4.

checks.q: A patient on prednisone for 8 months stopped it three days ago and now has a blood pressure of 74/40 that will not improve with 2 L of fluid. What do they need?
choices: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV with fluids and glucose
checks.why: This is adrenal crisis. Without cortisol the vasculature will not respond to fluids or catecholamines, so pressors alone fail. Steroid replacement is the fix, given alongside fluid and glucose.

checks.q: A patient makes 8 L of dilute urine a day with a serum sodium of 152 mEq/L. What is this?
checks.why: Huge dilute urine with a rising sodium means ADH is absent or ignored. SIADH is the opposite: low volume, concentrated urine, low sodium. Primary polydipsia produces dilute urine but a low sodium.

lessons.title: Glucose: insulin, diabetes, DKA and HHS
lessons.body:
## One hormone lowers it, four raise it

Fasting blood glucose runs `70–99 mg/dL`. Every cell needs glucose and the brain needs it continuously, because the brain cannot burn fat.

**Insulin**, from pancreatic beta cells, is the only hormone that lowers glucose. It opens the door: glucose into muscle and fat, storage as glycogen, building of protein and fat, and — the fact that decides DKA management — **it drives potassium into cells**.

**Glucagon**, from alpha cells, does the reverse. So do the other counter-regulatory hormones: epinephrine, cortisol and growth hormone. That is why a septic, injured or frightened patient runs a high glucose without being diabetic.

### Type 1 versus type 2

**Type 1** is autoimmune destruction of beta cells. There is no insulin at all. Usually diagnosed young and thin, always insulin-requiring, and these patients make ketones.

**Type 2** is insulin resistance: cells stop responding, the pancreas compensates with more insulin for years, then wears out. Usually older, usually overweight, and there is still enough circulating insulin to suppress ketone production — which is why type 2 tends toward HHS rather than DKA.

### DKA, step by step

1. **No effective insulin.** Glucose cannot enter cells. Serum glucose climbs, typically `350–800 mg/dL`.
2. **Cells starve, so the body burns fat.** Lipolysis floods the liver with free fatty acids.
3. **The liver makes ketones** — beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, acetone — and ketones are acids. Blood pH falls below `7.30`, bicarbonate below `18 mEq/L`, and the anion gap widens.
4. **The lungs compensate.** Deep, fast **Kussmaul respirations** blow off carbon dioxide, and acetone on the breath smells fruity.
5. **Glucose spills into urine** above about `180 mg/dL` and drags water out with it. This osmotic diuresis leaves the patient polyuric, polydipsic, and `5–10%` of body weight down — often a `4–6 L` deficit.
6. **Potassium plays a trick.** Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells into the serum, so the measured potassium reads normal or high — while the osmotic diuresis has been dumping potassium into the urine for hours. **Total body potassium is profoundly depleted.**

That trap is the entire reason the treatment order matters. Fluids first, isotonic crystalloid at roughly `15–20 mL/kg` in the first hour. Then an insulin infusion at about `0.1 units/kg/hr`. The instant insulin starts, potassium rushes back into cells and the serum level falls fast.

> **Key:** Hold the insulin if potassium is below `3.3 mEq/L` and replace potassium first, or you will drive the patient into an arrhythmia. Between `3.3` and `5.2`, replace potassium alongside the insulin rather than after it.

When the glucose falls to about `200 mg/dL`, add dextrose to the fluids and **keep the insulin running**, because the insulin is treating the acidosis, not the sugar. Bicarbonate is generally reserved for a pH below `6.9`.

### HHS: the type 2 version

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state builds over days rather than hours. Glucose is far higher — commonly above `600 mg/dL` and not rarely above `1000` — serum osmolality climbs above `320 mOsm/kg`, and there is **little or no ketosis** because residual insulin still blocks lipolysis. The presentation is profound dehydration and altered mental status rather than air hunger. Fluid deficits reach `8–12 L` and mortality runs higher than DKA.

### Hypoglycemia

Below about `70 mg/dL`, symptoms arrive in two waves.

- **Adrenergic first**, roughly `55–70`: sweating, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger. That is epinephrine doing its job. Beta blockers erase these warnings.
- **Neuroglycopenic next**, under about `50`: confusion, slurred speech, focal deficits that mimic stroke, seizure, coma.

**Whipple's triad** confirms the diagnosis: symptoms are present, a low glucose is documented, and the symptoms resolve when glucose is corrected.

> **On shift:** Check a glucose on every altered patient, every seizure, every stroke alert and every "just not acting right." It takes `15 seconds` and it is the most commonly missed reversible cause of altered mental status.
keyPoints: Insulin is the only hormone that lowers glucose and it also drives potassium into cells.
DKA: no insulin, lipolysis, ketoacids, Kussmaul breathing, osmotic diuresis, and a 4–6 L fluid deficit.
The DKA potassium reads normal while total body potassium is empty — hold insulin below 3.3 mEq/L.
HHS is type 2: glucose often above 600, osmolality above 320, minimal ketones, 8–12 L down.
Hypoglycemia goes adrenergic then neuroglycopenic; beta blockers delete the warning stage.

checks.q: A DKA patient's initial potassium is 4.6 mEq/L. What is true?
choices: Potassium is normal and needs no attention
Total body potassium is depleted and the level will fall once insulin starts
Insulin will raise the serum potassium
Potassium should only be given above 5.5
checks.why: Acidosis has shifted potassium out of cells, masking hours of urinary losses. Insulin reverses that shift and the serum level drops fast, so potassium is replaced alongside the infusion.

checks.q: In DKA the glucose reaches 190 mg/dL but the anion gap is still 18. What now?
choices: Add dextrose to the fluids and continue the insulin infusion
checks.why: Insulin is treating the ketoacidosis, not the sugar, so it continues until the gap closes. Dextrose is added so the glucose does not crash while the insulin runs. Bicarbonate is generally reserved for a pH below 6.9.

checks.q: Why is HHS not ketotic?
choices: Residual insulin is still enough to suppress lipolysis, even though it cannot control glucose
The glucose is too high for ketone formation
checks.why: It takes very little insulin to block fat breakdown, and type 2 patients still have some. That is why they reach extreme glucose and osmolality without the acidosis of DKA.

cards.front: What are the four jobs of the GI tract?
cards.back: Digestion (break food down), absorption (move it into blood or lymph), motility (push it along), and elimination of what is left.

cards.front: What are the three phases of swallowing, and which one protects the airway?
cards.back: Oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (involuntary, seals the nose and larynx, breathing stops about 1 second), esophageal (peristalsis, 5-10 seconds). The pharyngeal phase protects the airway.

cards.front: Which four substances does the stomach secrete, and which cell makes each?
cards.back: Parietal cells: hydrochloric acid (pH 1.5-3.5) and intrinsic factor. Chief cells: pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin. Mucous cells: the bicarbonate-rich protective mucus layer.

cards.front: What two things most commonly strip the stomach's protective mucus layer?
cards.back: Helicobacter pylori infection and chronic NSAID use. Both lead to peptic ulcer disease by letting acid and pepsin reach the gastric wall.

cards.front: Where in the small intestine is each nutrient absorbed?
cards.back: Duodenum: iron, calcium, folate. Jejunum: most carbohydrate, protein, fat and water-soluble vitamins. Ileum: vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor, and bile salts for recycling.

cards.front: How much fluid enters the colon daily and how much leaves as stool?
cards.back: About 1-1.5 L of liquid chyme arrives; about 100-200 mL leaves as stool. The colon's main job is reclaiming water and electrolytes.

cards.front: Why does a leaking lower esophageal sphincter cause a diagnostic trap?
cards.back: GERD produces burning chest pain that is indistinguishable from myocardial infarction. Relief with antacids does not rule out a heart attack.

cards.front: Name seven jobs of the liver.
cards.back: Bile (500-1000 mL/day), clotting factors, albumin (10-15 g/day), glycogen storage and glucose release, drug metabolism via P450, ammonia to urea, and bilirubin conjugation.

cards.front: Why does liver failure cause ascites?
cards.back: The liver stops making albumin, so oncotic pressure falls and fluid leaves the vessels. Portal hypertension pushes it into the peritoneal cavity.

cards.front: What causes hepatic encephalopathy and what is its signature physical finding?
cards.back: Ammonia the failing liver can no longer convert to urea. The signature finding is asterixis, the flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, along with confusion progressing to coma.

cards.front: At roughly what bilirubin level does jaundice become visible?
cards.back: Around a total bilirubin of 2.5-3 mg/dL. The sclera yellow before the skin does.

cards.front: What does pain plus jaundice plus fever mean in a patient with gallstones?
cards.back: Ascending cholangitis: a stone obstructing the common bile duct with infection behind it. A surgical and endoscopic emergency, not simple biliary colic.

cards.front: How does the pancreas split its exocrine and endocrine work?
cards.back: About 99% is exocrine: 1-1.5 L/day of amylase, lipase, trypsin and bicarbonate. About 1% is islets of Langerhans: beta cells make insulin, alpha cells glucagon, delta cells somatostatin.

cards.front: Why is the spleen clinically important in trauma and in infection?
cards.back: It is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma, and it makes antibodies against encapsulated bacteria. Asplenic patients can go from cough to septic shock in hours.

cards.front: Which organs sit in each abdominal quadrant?
cards.back: RUQ: liver, gallbladder, duodenum, pancreas head. LUQ: stomach, spleen, pancreas tail. RLQ: appendix, cecum, right adnexa. LLQ: sigmoid colon, left adnexa. Kidneys sit posteriorly on both sides.

cards.front: What three serious diagnoses live in the epigastrium?
cards.back: Pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, and inferior wall myocardial infarction. Epigastric pain is never automatically indigestion.

cards.front: How does visceral pain differ from parietal pain?
cards.back: Visceral pain is dull, crampy, midline, poorly localized and comes with nausea and sweating. Parietal pain is sharp, constant and pointable because the parietal peritoneum has precise somatic mapping.

cards.front: Why does appendicitis pain migrate, and where does it end up?
cards.back: It starts as vague periumbilical visceral pain at the T10 level, then over 12-24 hours inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum and the pain becomes sharp at McBurney's point.

cards.front: Where is McBurney's point?
cards.back: One third of the way along a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine toward the umbilicus. Focal tenderness there suggests appendicitis.

cards.front: Give the referred pain map for four abdominal organs.
cards.back: Diaphragm or spleen: left shoulder (Kehr's sign, phrenic C3-C5). Gallbladder: right shoulder or scapula. Pancreas: straight through to the back. Ureteral stone: flank to groin.

cards.front: How do you elicit Murphy's sign and what does a positive mean?
cards.back: Press under the right costal margin and ask for a deep breath. If the patient stops mid-inspiration, it is positive and suggests acute cholecystitis.

cards.front: What are the four classic findings of peritonitis?
cards.back: Guarding, rigidity (a board-like belly), rebound tenderness (worse on release), and absent bowel sounds from ileus.

cards.front: How does posture separate peritonitis from colic?
cards.back: Peritonitis patients lie perfectly still because motion drags inflamed surfaces. Colic patients writhe and cannot get comfortable because a hollow organ is squeezing.

cards.front: What causes most small bowel obstructions, and what causes large bowel obstruction?
cards.back: Small bowel: adhesions from prior surgery, about 60%, then hernias and tumors. Large bowel: cancer, volvulus and diverticular stricture.

cards.front: How do small and large bowel obstruction differ in presentation?
cards.back: Small bowel: early bilious vomiting, moderate distension, cramping every 3-5 minutes, late obstipation. Large bowel: late feculent vomiting, marked distension, cramping every 10-15 minutes, early obstipation.

cards.front: What signals that a bowel obstruction has strangulated?
cards.back: Crampy pain becomes constant, plus fever, tachycardia and a rising lactate. Blood supply is cut off and bowel dies within hours.

cards.front: What anatomic landmark divides upper from lower GI bleeding?
cards.back: The ligament of Treitz at the duodenojejunal junction. Above it is upper GI bleeding; below it is lower GI bleeding.

cards.front: How much blood and how much time does it take to produce melena?
cards.back: As little as 50 mL of blood and roughly 14 hours in the gut. Melena is black, tarry and foul-smelling because acid and bacteria have digested the blood.

cards.front: Why does the BUN rise in an upper GI bleed?
cards.back: Blood protein is digested and absorbed as a nitrogen load. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 30:1 with GI bleeding points to a source above the ligament of Treitz.

cards.front: What six jobs does the kidney do?
cards.back: Clears nitrogen waste, balances water, balances electrolytes, manages acid-base, regulates blood pressure via renin, and makes erythropoietin while activating vitamin D.

cards.front: What is a normal GFR, and how much is filtered each day?
cards.back: About 100-125 mL/min, roughly 180 L filtered per day. Since urine output is 1-2 L, more than 99% is reabsorbed downstream.

cards.front: What does the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorb, and at what glucose does it saturate?
cards.back: About 65% of sodium and water, plus essentially all glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. Glucose transport saturates near a serum glucose of 180 mg/dL, which is when sugar spills into urine.

cards.front: How does the loop of Henle let you concentrate urine?
cards.back: The descending limb loses water only; the thick ascending limb pumps out sodium, potassium and chloride but is waterproof. That builds a salty medulla, the gradient that concentrated urine depends on.

cards.front: What do aldosterone and ADH each do at the collecting duct?
cards.back: Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium and secretes potassium: save salt, dump potassium. ADH inserts water channels so water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.

cards.front: Where does each diuretic class act and what does it do to potassium?
cards.back: Loops at the thick ascending limb, lower potassium. Thiazides at the distal tubule, lower potassium. Potassium-sparing agents at the collecting duct, raise potassium. Acetazolamide at the proximal tubule, mild loss.

cards.front: Trace the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway.
cards.back: Low renal perfusion releases renin, which makes angiotensin I. ACE, mostly in the lung, makes angiotensin II, a vasoconstrictor that also triggers aldosterone and ADH. ACE inhibitors and ARBs block this and raise potassium.

cards.front: How is total body water distributed in a 70 kg adult?
cards.back: About 60% of body weight, roughly 42 L. Two thirds (about 28 L) is intracellular; one third (about 14 L) is extracellular, split into about 11 L interstitial and about 3 L plasma.

cards.front: Which cation dominates inside cells and which dominates outside?
cards.back: Potassium inside, sodium outside. That is why serum potassium reflects only about 2% of body stores, and why sodium sets extracellular osmolality.

cards.front: What is normal serum osmolality and how do you estimate it?
cards.back: 275-295 mOsm/kg. Estimate with 2 times sodium, plus glucose divided by 18, plus BUN divided by 2.8. Sodium dominates the equation.

cards.front: Why is serum sodium a water question rather than a salt question?
cards.back: Sodium is a concentration, not a total. A low sodium usually means too much water for the salt present. Volume status is judged by blood pressure, heart rate, urine output and neck veins instead.

cards.front: What is third spacing and why is it deceptive?
cards.back: Fluid that is inside the body but not inside the vessels, as in bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, burns and ascites. The patient can gain several kilograms of weight and still be in shock.

cards.front: Where does normal saline go, and where does D5W go?
cards.back: Normal saline (154 mEq/L sodium and chloride) stays in the extracellular fluid; only about a quarter stays intravascular. D5W becomes free water once the sugar is burned, so only about one twelfth stays intravascular.

cards.front: What is the minimum acceptable urine output in an adult and a child?
cards.back: 0.5 mL/kg/hr in an adult and 1 mL/kg/hr in a child. It is the cheapest continuous readout of whether perfusion is adequate.

cards.front: What is the normal sodium range and what does hyponatremia do to the brain?
cards.back: 135-145 mEq/L. Low sodium lets water into brain cells and swells them: headache and confusion below 125, seizures below 120 or after any rapid drop.

cards.front: How fast may hyponatremia be corrected, and why?
cards.back: No faster than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours. Faster correction risks osmotic demyelination, a permanent brainstem injury. The exception is an actively seizing patient, who gets small 3% saline boluses.

cards.front: List the causes of hyperkalemia you will actually meet.
cards.back: Renal failure and missed dialysis, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, crush injury and rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, acidosis, and a hemolyzed specimen.

cards.front: What is the ECG progression of rising potassium?
cards.back: Peaked narrow T waves near 5.5-6.5, then flattened P waves with a long PR near 6.5-7.5, then a widening QRS near 7-8, then a sine wave and ventricular fibrillation or asystole above 8.

cards.front: Give the hyperkalemia treatment order and the purpose of each step.
cards.back: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV stabilizes the membrane in 1-3 minutes but lowers nothing. Insulin 10 units with 25 g dextrose and albuterol 10-20 mg shift it into cells. Diuretics, binders and dialysis actually remove it.

cards.front: What does hypokalemia look like on the ECG and who gets it?
cards.back: Flattened T waves, prominent U waves and ventricular arrhythmias below 3.5 mEq/L. Causes are diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea and insulin. It cannot be corrected without also fixing magnesium.

cards.front: How do you correct total calcium for a low albumin?
cards.back: Add 0.8 mg/dL to the calcium for every 1 g/dL the albumin sits below 4 g/dL. Only ionized calcium (4.6-5.3 mg/dL) is biologically active; about 40% of calcium is bound to albumin.

cards.front: Contrast the signs of hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia.
cards.back: Low: perioral and fingertip tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, tetany, long QT, laryngospasm. High: stones, bones, groans and psychiatric overtones, with a short QT.

cards.front: Which electrolyte causes torsades de pointes and how is it treated?
cards.back: Low magnesium (normal 1.5-2.5 mg/dL). Treat torsades with magnesium sulfate 1-2 g IV. Low magnesium also makes potassium impossible to replete.

cards.front: How does the kidney handle acid, and how is that different from the lung?
cards.back: The lung blows off carbon dioxide in minutes. The kidney works over hours to days: reabsorbs filtered bicarbonate, generates new bicarbonate, and excretes hydrogen buffered as ammonium and phosphate.

cards.front: How is acute kidney injury defined?
cards.back: A creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a 50% rise within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hours.

cards.front: How do you tell pre-renal AKI from acute tubular necrosis at the bedside?
cards.back: Pre-renal: BUN-to-creatinine above 20:1, concentrated urine, low urine sodium, responds to fluid. ATN: ratio back to 10-15:1, urine sodium above 40, muddy brown granular casts, does not respond to fluid.

cards.front: What causes post-renal AKI and why does it matter most?
cards.back: Prostate enlargement, stones, tumors or a clotted catheter. It is the fastest AKI to reverse: a bladder scan and a catheter can fix it in minutes, and it is the one most often missed.

cards.front: How is chronic kidney disease staged?
cards.back: By GFR in mL/min/1.73 m2: stage 1 is 90 or above with damage, stage 2 is 60-89, stage 3 is 30-59, stage 4 is 15-29, and stage 5 is under 15 or dialysis dependence.

cards.front: Rank the three hemodialysis access types and give the rules for the access arm.
cards.back: Fistula (best, matures in 2-3 months), graft (2-3 weeks), tunneled catheter (immediate, highest infection risk). No cuff, no IV, no draw, no tourniquet on that arm. Feel for a thrill, listen for a bruit.

cards.front: What two emergencies does a missed dialysis session produce?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia that can arrest the heart, and volume overload that floods the lungs. Any dialysis patient who skipped a session and feels weak or breathless gets an ECG immediately.

cards.front: What separates cystitis, pyelonephritis and a kidney stone?
cards.back: Cystitis: burning, frequency, suprapubic ache, no fever. Pyelonephritis: fever, chills, flank pain, CVA tenderness. Stone: sudden colicky flank-to-groin pain with hematuria in a patient who cannot lie still.

cards.front: How do you read any hypothalamic-pituitary axis from two lab values?
cards.back: High stimulating hormone with low final hormone means the target gland failed. Low stimulating hormone with high final hormone means the gland is running on its own. That single rule covers thyroid and adrenal testing.

cards.front: Which hormones come from the posterior pituitary, and where are they made?
cards.back: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin. The posterior pituitary manufactures nothing; both are made in the hypothalamus and only stored and released there.

cards.front: Contrast hyperthyroid and hypothyroid signs.
cards.back: Hyper: weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, anxiety, tremor, diarrhea, warm moist skin. Hypo: weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia, depression, slowed thought, constipation, dry coarse skin.

cards.front: Describe thyroid storm and myxedema coma.
cards.back: Storm: temperature above 40 C, heart rate over 140, agitation or delirium, usually triggered by infection or surgery. Myxedema coma: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention, hyponatremia, depressed consciousness.

cards.front: What does the adrenal cortex make, and what does the medulla make?
cards.back: Cortex: aldosterone (salt), cortisol (sugar and stress response) and androgens (sex). Medulla: catecholamines, epinephrine and norepinephrine.

cards.front: What does adrenal crisis look like and how is it treated?
cards.back: Hypotension unresponsive to fluid and pressors, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, vomiting and abdominal pain in a steroid-dependent patient. Treat with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV plus fluids and glucose.

cards.front: What does parathyroid hormone do?
cards.back: Raises calcium three ways: pulls it from bone, reabsorbs it in the distal tubule, and activates vitamin D in the kidney so the gut absorbs more. It lowers phosphate.

cards.front: Compare SIADH with diabetes insipidus.
cards.back: SIADH: too much ADH, concentrated low-volume urine, low serum sodium, treated with fluid restriction. Diabetes insipidus: too little or ineffective ADH, 3-20 L of dilute urine daily, high sodium, treated with desmopressin and free water.

cards.front: What is the only hormone that lowers glucose, and what else does it do?
cards.back: Insulin, from pancreatic beta cells. It moves glucose into muscle and fat, stores glycogen, builds protein and fat, and drives potassium into cells. Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and growth hormone all raise glucose.

cards.front: Why does type 1 diabetes cause DKA while type 2 causes HHS?
cards.back: Type 1 has no insulin, so fat breakdown runs unchecked and ketoacids accumulate. Type 2 has enough residual insulin to block lipolysis but not enough to control glucose, so osmolality climbs without ketosis.

cards.front: Walk the DKA mechanism from missing insulin to Kussmaul breathing.
cards.back: No insulin, so cells starve and fat is burned. The liver converts fatty acids into ketoacids, pH falls below 7.30 and bicarbonate below 18, the anion gap widens, and the lungs compensate with deep fast Kussmaul respirations.

cards.front: Why does the potassium in DKA lie to you?
cards.back: Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells so the serum level reads normal or high, while osmotic diuresis has been dumping potassium in urine for hours. Total body potassium is severely depleted and falls further once insulin starts.

cards.front: Give the DKA treatment sequence with numbers.
cards.back: Isotonic crystalloid 15-20 mL/kg in the first hour, then insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hr. Hold insulin if potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L. Add dextrose when glucose reaches about 200 mg/dL and keep the insulin running until the gap closes.

cards.front: What numbers define HHS and how big is the fluid deficit?
cards.back: Glucose commonly above 600 mg/dL and sometimes above 1000, serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, minimal or no ketones. Fluid deficits reach 8-12 L and mortality exceeds DKA.

cards.front: What are the two symptom waves of hypoglycemia, and what is Whipple's triad?
cards.back: Adrenergic at 55-70 mg/dL: sweating, tremor, tachycardia, hunger. Neuroglycopenic under 50: confusion, slurred speech, focal deficits, seizure. Whipple's triad is symptoms, a documented low glucose, and relief with correction.

quiz.q: Which segment of bowel is the only site that absorbs vitamin B12?
quiz.why: B12 must be bound to intrinsic factor, and receptors for that complex exist only in the terminal ileum. The duodenum takes iron, calcium and folate; the jejunum takes most everything else; the colon absorbs water, not vitamins.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old with a recent stroke coughs and turns red every time she drinks thin liquids. Which phase of swallowing has failed?
quiz.why: The pharyngeal phase is the involuntary reflex that seals the nasopharynx and covers the larynx. Stroke blunts it and liquids enter the airway. The oral phase is voluntary and the esophageal phase happens after the airway is already protected.

quiz.q: A patient who takes ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for arthritis develops burning epigastric pain and black stools. Which protective mechanism was lost?
choices: The bicarbonate-rich mucus layer over the gastric lining
Pancreatic bicarbonate delivery to the duodenum
quiz.why: NSAIDs strip the gastric mucus and bicarbonate barrier, letting acid and pepsin reach the wall and ulcerate it. LES tone causes reflux, not ulcers. Intrinsic factor affects B12 years later and pancreatic bicarbonate protects the duodenum, not the stomach.

quiz.q: Where is bile stored and concentrated between meals?
choices: In the head of the pancreas
quiz.why: The gallbladder holds 30-50 mL of concentrated bile and releases it when cholecystokinin responds to fat in the duodenum. The liver makes bile continuously but does not store it; the ducts are conduits.

quiz.q: A patient with cirrhosis is confused, and when he holds his arms out his hands flap. What is causing this?
choices: Ammonia the failing liver can no longer convert to urea
Low albumin lowering cerebral oncotic pressure
Bilirubin deposited in the basal ganglia
quiz.why: Asterixis with confusion is hepatic encephalopathy from accumulated ammonia. Low albumin produces ascites and edema, not encephalopathy. Bilirubin causes jaundice, and while cirrhotics can become hypoglycemic, that does not produce asterixis.

quiz.q: Why does a cirrhotic patient bleed catastrophically from esophageal varices?
choices: The varices are arterial and under systemic pressure
Portal hypertension raises pressure in the varices while the failing liver cannot make clotting factors
Bile salts in the blood dissolve platelet plugs
quiz.why: It is two failures at once: high portal pressure driving the bleed and no clotting factors to stop it. Varices are dilated veins, not arteries. Bile salts and ammonia do not act on the clotting cascade in this way.

quiz.q: You press under the right costal margin and the patient stops mid-inspiration. What does this suggest?
quiz.why: That is Murphy's sign, inspiratory arrest from an inflamed gallbladder meeting your hand. Appendicitis shows McBurney and Rovsing signs, diverticulitis is left lower quadrant, and pancreatitis is epigastric with pain boring to the back.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old had dull pain around the navel 14 hours ago; now it is sharp and fixed in the right lower quadrant with rebound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Migration from vague visceral periumbilical pain to sharp localized right lower quadrant pain over 12-24 hours is the appendicitis signature. Ovarian cyst rupture is usually sudden and focal from the start, gastroenteritis is diffuse and crampy, and pyelonephritis brings fever and CVA tenderness.

quiz.q: A patient kicked in the left flank complains of left shoulder pain with a normal shoulder exam. What is this called and what does it mean?
choices: Kehr's sign, from blood irritating the left diaphragm
quiz.why: The phrenic nerve carries diaphragmatic irritation to the C3-C5 shoulder dermatomes, so free blood under the left diaphragm reads as shoulder pain. Murphy and Rovsing are abdominal palpation findings; Cullen's sign is periumbilical bruising.

quiz.q: What causes about 60% of small bowel obstructions in adults?
quiz.why: Adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction. Hernias are second. Colon cancer and volvulus obstruct the large bowel and present with late feculent vomiting and marked distension instead.

quiz.q: A patient has black tarry stools, a BUN of 52 mg/dL and a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL. Where is the bleeding?
quiz.why: Melena plus a BUN-to-creatinine ratio near 47:1 means an upper source: digested blood protein is absorbed as a nitrogen load. Colonic and anorectal bleeding presents as bright red or maroon blood and does not raise the BUN that way.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old with sudden severe epigastric pain lies absolutely motionless, has a board-like abdomen and rebound tenderness. What does the posture tell you?
choices: Peritoneal irritation, most likely a perforated viscus
quiz.why: Peritonitis patients stay still because any movement drags inflamed surfaces across each other. Colic patients, including those with stones or early obstruction, writhe and cannot get comfortable. Gastroenteritis does not produce rigidity.

quiz.q: What is a normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult?
quiz.why: Roughly 100-125 mL/min filters about 180 L per day. 1200 mL/min is renal blood flow, not filtration. 25 mL/min would be stage 4 chronic kidney disease.

quiz.q: Furosemide exerts its effect at which part of the nephron?
choices: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
quiz.why: Loop diuretics block the sodium-potassium-chloride transporter in the thick ascending limb, which is why they are the most potent class and why they destroy the concentrating gradient. Thiazides act distally and spironolactone at the collecting duct.

quiz.q: A patient with heart failure and a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL is started on a new diuretic and returns with a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L. Which drug is most likely responsible?
quiz.why: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the collecting duct, so sodium is lost and potassium is retained, which is dangerous in renal impairment. Loops and thiazides lower potassium; acetazolamide causes only mild loss.

quiz.q: Why is 5% dextrose in water a poor resuscitation fluid for a hemorrhaging patient?
choices: It is hypertonic and pulls water out of cells
It has no sodium so it causes immediate hypernatremia
It causes a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Once the dextrose is metabolized it behaves as free water and spreads through every compartment
quiz.why: D5W is isotonic only in the bag; after the sugar is burned, roughly one twelfth stays intravascular. Hyperchloremic acidosis is a large-volume normal saline problem. Free water lowers sodium rather than raising it.

quiz.q: About what fraction of total body water sits inside cells?
quiz.why: Two thirds of total body water is intracellular, roughly 28 L in a 70 kg adult. The remaining third is extracellular and only about 3 L of that is plasma, which is why intravascular volume is so easy to lose.

quiz.q: A pancreatitis patient has gained 4 kg since admission but is tachycardic at 122 with a blood pressure of 86/50. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: He is fluid overloaded and needs a diuretic
Fluid has third-spaced out of the vessels, so he is intravascularly depleted despite the weight gain
His serum sodium must be critically low
The weight gain indicates adequate resuscitation
quiz.why: Pancreatitis drives massive third spacing into the retroperitoneum and gut. The fluid is inside the body but not in the vessels. Diuresing him would deepen the shock, and the sodium can be entirely normal.

quiz.q: A malnourished patient has a total calcium of 7.6 mg/dL and an albumin of 2.0 g/dL. How should you interpret the calcium?
choices: Corrected calcium is about 9.2 mg/dL, so the ionized calcium is probably normal
Total calcium cannot be interpreted without an ionized level
quiz.why: Albumin is 2 g/dL below 4, so add 0.8 twice: 7.6 plus 1.6 equals about 9.2. About 40% of calcium is protein-bound and inactive. Treating on the uncorrected number would be an unnecessary intervention.

quiz.q: A patient on a QT-prolonging antipsychotic develops a twisting polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. What is the drug of choice?
quiz.why: Torsades de pointes is treated with magnesium regardless of the serum magnesium level. Calcium stabilizes membranes in hyperkalemia, bicarbonate treats sodium channel blockade, and IV potassium is never pushed.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.6 mEq/L and a QRS of 150 ms. Which intervention comes first?
