choices: Regular insulin 10 units with 25 g dextrose
Arranging emergent hemodialysis before any drug
quiz.why: Calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane within 1-3 minutes and prevents arrest while everything else is arranged. Insulin and albuterol shift potassium but take 15-30 minutes, and dialysis takes far longer to set up.

quiz.q: What is the earliest ECG change of hyperkalemia?
quiz.why: Peaked T waves appear around 5.5-6.5 mEq/L, followed by flattened P waves and PR prolongation, then QRS widening, then the sine wave. U waves belong to hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

quiz.q: A hypotensive patient has a BUN of 64 mg/dL, a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL and a urine sodium of 12 mEq/L. Which category of acute kidney injury is this?
quiz.why: A ratio of 40:1 with avid sodium retention means the tubules still function and are hoarding, which is pre-renal and fluid-responsive. ATN loses that ability and shows urine sodium above 40 with muddy brown casts. Obstruction is confirmed by bladder scan and imaging.

quiz.q: A patient has an arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm. What is the rule for that arm?
choices: Draw blood distal to the thrill only
Use a pediatric cuff placed above the fistula
Start an IV in the fistula only during emergencies
Keep blood pressure cuffs, IVs, tourniquets and blood draws off that arm entirely
quiz.why: Anything that compresses or punctures the access risks thrombosing it and sending the patient to surgery. There is no safe distal draw, no safe cuff placement, and no routine emergency exception on that arm.

quiz.q: A 27-year-old with two days of burning urination now has a temperature of 38.9 C and pain when you percuss her flank. What has changed?
choices: The infection has ascended to the kidney, which is pyelonephritis
She has formed an obstructing stone
quiz.why: Fever with costovertebral angle tenderness marks kidney involvement, which changes treatment from oral antibiotics at home to IV antibiotics and possible admission. Cystitis alone does not cause fever or CVA tenderness, and a stone produces colicky pain, not steady flank tenderness with fever.

quiz.q: A patient has a TSH of 18 mIU/L and a free T4 below the reference range. What does this indicate?
choices: Primary hypothyroidism, with the pituitary pushing a failing gland
quiz.why: A high stimulating hormone with a low final hormone localizes the problem to the target gland. Pituitary failure would show a low or inappropriately normal TSH with a low T4. Graves disease suppresses TSH and raises T4.

quiz.q: A patient who took prednisone 20 mg daily for six months stopped abruptly, then developed vomiting and a blood pressure of 76/40 that does not improve after 2 L of crystalloid. What does she need?
choices: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV with fluids and glucose
An insulin infusion for the hyperkalemia
quiz.why: This is adrenal crisis. Without cortisol the vasculature does not respond to fluid or catecholamines, so pressors alone fail. Steroid replacement restores that responsiveness, and glucose and sodium are corrected alongside it.

quiz.q: A patient after pituitary surgery makes 8 L of dilute urine per day with a serum sodium of 152 mEq/L. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: Large volumes of dilute urine with a rising sodium means ADH is missing or ignored, which fits pituitary surgery. SIADH is the mirror image: low-volume concentrated urine with a low sodium. Polydipsia and thiazides both lower sodium.

quiz.q: A patient in DKA has an initial potassium of 4.8 mEq/L. What is the most accurate statement?
choices: Total body potassium is depleted and the serum level will fall sharply once insulin starts
Potassium is normal and requires no attention
Potassium should only be replaced if it exceeds 5.5 mEq/L
Insulin will raise the serum potassium
quiz.why: Acidosis shifted potassium out of cells and masked hours of urinary losses. Insulin reverses that shift and the serum level drops quickly, so potassium is replaced alongside the infusion rather than after a crash.

quiz.q: Below which potassium level should the insulin infusion be held in DKA until potassium is replaced?
quiz.why: Below 3.3 mEq/L, insulin will drive potassium into cells and can precipitate a lethal arrhythmia, so potassium comes first. Between 3.3 and 5.2 it is replaced alongside the insulin. Waiting until 2.0 is far too late.

quiz.q: A 78-year-old with type 2 diabetes is lethargic. Glucose is 1080 mg/dL, osmolality 345 mOsm/kg, and ketones are minimal with a pH of 7.36. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: Extreme glucose and osmolality with minimal ketosis and a normal pH is HHS, which happens because residual insulin still suppresses lipolysis. DKA requires acidosis and ketones. The glucose value rules out hypoglycemia outright.

quiz.q: A diabetic taking metoprolol is found confused with a glucose of 44 mg/dL but is not sweaty or tremulous. Why were there no warning symptoms?
choices: The glucose meter is unreliable at low values
Neuroglycopenic symptoms always precede adrenergic ones
Beta blockers raise the glucose threshold for symptoms
The beta blocker masks the adrenergic warning stage, so the first visible sign is neuroglycopenic
quiz.why: Sweating, tremor and tachycardia are epinephrine effects that beta blockade suppresses, so these patients skip the warning wave and present already confused. Adrenergic symptoms normally come first, at about 55-70 mg/dL.

scenarios.title: Reasoning it out: the dialysis patient who skipped Friday
scenarios.intro:
Work this one as physiology, not as a checklist. A 58-year-old man has end-stage kidney disease and dialyzes Monday, Wednesday and Friday. He missed Friday because his ride fell through. It is now Sunday afternoon and he says his legs feel heavy and his arms feel weak. He has a left forearm arteriovenous fistula.

At each step, decide what the physiology demands before you decide what to do.

steps.prompt:
He is awake and conversational but says he feels "like a wet towel." He denies chest pain. You have two minutes before anyone else is available.

What is the single highest-yield action right now?

choices.text: Place him on the cardiac monitor and obtain a 12-lead ECG
choices.feedback: Correct. In a patient who missed dialysis, hyperkalemia is the leading cause of sudden death, and the ECG reports on the potassium faster than any laboratory. The ECG is the potassium meter you already have in the room.

choices.text: Draw a basic metabolic panel and wait for the potassium result
choices.feedback: Reasonable, and the panel must be sent. But laboratory turnaround is typically 30-60 minutes, and a potassium of 8 can arrest a heart in that window. Send it and get the ECG while you wait.

choices.text: Give a 1 L normal saline bolus for the weakness
choices.feedback: Harmful. He makes little or no urine and is already two days behind on fluid removal. A liter of saline has nowhere to go except his lungs, and it does nothing for the potassium that is actually causing the weakness.

choices.text: Order a chest radiograph for the low oxygen saturation
choices.feedback: It will probably show pulmonary edema and it is worth getting, but it does not change what you do in the next two minutes. Order it after the ECG, not before.

steps.prompt:
The ECG shows a heart rate of 56, tall symmetric peaked T waves in the precordial leads, P waves you can barely identify, and a QRS duration of 148 ms.

What does this tracing tell you about his potassium?

choices.text: He is past the peaked-T stage into conduction failure, so the potassium is likely 7 or above
choices.feedback: Right. The ladder is peaked T waves near 5.5-6.5, then flat P waves and PR prolongation near 6.5-7.5, then QRS widening near 7-8. Losing P waves with a wide QRS puts him high on that ladder and close to a sine wave.

choices.text: Peaked T waves alone, so the potassium is probably 5.5-6.0
choices.feedback: You stopped reading too early. Peaked T waves alone would be 5.5-6.5, but the vanishing P waves and the 148 ms QRS are the next two rungs. Each additional finding moves the estimate higher and the urgency up.

choices.text: This is an acute anterior myocardial infarction; activate the catheterization laboratory
choices.feedback: Dangerous anchoring. Hyperkalemic T waves are tall, narrow and symmetric with a pointed peak; ischemic hyperacute T waves are broad-based and come with ST changes. Missing hyperkalemia here costs the patient the treatment that would save him.

choices.text: ECG changes cannot estimate potassium, so the tracing adds nothing
choices.feedback: Not true, and treating it as true is lethal. The ECG will not give you a decimal value, but the pattern reliably tells you whether the membrane is already unstable, which is the only question that matters before the laboratory calls.

steps.prompt:
The laboratory calls a critical potassium of 7.4 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, creatinine 9.8 mg/dL. He is still awake.

What goes in first, and why?

choices.text: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV
choices.feedback: Correct, and understand what it does. Calcium raises the threshold potential and restores the gap between resting and threshold potential, stabilizing the myocardium within 1-3 minutes. It lowers the potassium by exactly zero. It buys you the time to do everything else.

choices.text: Regular insulin 10 units IV with 25 g dextrose
choices.feedback: This is the right second move but the wrong first one. Insulin takes about 15 minutes to work. With a 148 ms QRS, the heart may not have 15 minutes. Protect the membrane, then shift.

choices.text: Call the nephrologist for emergent dialysis and wait for the team
choices.feedback: Dialysis is the definitive treatment and that call must happen, but mobilizing a machine and a nurse takes 30-90 minutes. Waiting without stabilizing the membrane is how these patients arrest in the hallway.

choices.text: Give an oral potassium binder and recheck in two hours
choices.feedback: Far too slow for an unstable ECG. Binders work over hours in the gut and are an adjunct, not an emergency treatment. This choice treats a number and ignores a heart that is minutes from a sine wave.

steps.prompt:
Calcium is in and the QRS narrows to 112 ms within three minutes.

What is the next move, and what is the trap in the improvement you just saw?

choices.text: Give insulin 10 units IV with 25 g dextrose and albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized to shift potassium into cells
choices.feedback: Correct, and note the trap: calcium narrowed the QRS without removing a single milliequivalent. Its effect fades in 30-60 minutes. Shifting buys 4-6 hours, and glucose must be monitored because the insulin outlasts the dextrose.

choices.text: Repeat calcium every five minutes until the ECG is fully normal
choices.feedback: Calcium can be repeated if the QRS re-widens, but chasing a normal-looking ECG with more calcium ignores the fact that the potassium has not moved. You are treating the monitor, not the patient.

choices.text: Nothing further is needed since the QRS normalized
choices.feedback: This is the single most dangerous misunderstanding in hyperkalemia. Calcium is a membrane shield with a 30-60 minute half-life. The potassium is unchanged at 7.4 and the patient will deteriorate again, often without warning.

choices.text: Give furosemide 80 mg IV to drive potassium out in the urine
choices.feedback: Not useful here. He has a creatinine of 9.8 and makes essentially no urine, so there is no diuresis to drive. In a patient with residual kidney function this would be a reasonable removal step.

steps.prompt:
Insulin and albuterol are running. He now has crackles halfway up both lung fields and his oxygen saturation has drifted to 88% on room air.

What does he actually need to survive the day?

choices.text: Emergent hemodialysis, because it is the only intervention that removes both the potassium and the fluid
choices.feedback: Correct. Everything to this point was a holding action. Dialysis is the only treatment that solves both stacked problems at once: it pulls the potassium out of the body and pulls the volume off his lungs. Oxygen and non-invasive ventilation support him until the machine is running.

choices.text: Another liter of normal saline to improve his blood pressure
choices.feedback: Harmful. His pressure is 176/98 and his lungs are already wet. Adding volume to an anuric patient in pulmonary edema converts a difficult case into an intubation.

choices.text: Repeat the insulin and dextrose hourly and admit him to a medical floor
choices.feedback: Repeated shifting has real risks, mainly hypoglycemia, and it never removes potassium. Serial shifting without a removal plan is a patient waiting to rebound on a unit with less monitoring than he needs.

choices.text: Place him on oxygen and non-invasive positive pressure ventilation while dialysis is arranged
choices.feedback: A good supportive move and correct to do in parallel, but it is not the answer to the question. Positive pressure improves the oxygenation and the work of breathing; only dialysis fixes what is causing both problems.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **a missed dialysis session is two emergencies stacked on one patient.** Hyperkalemia can arrest the heart in minutes, and volume overload can drown the lungs over hours.

The reasoning chain: no kidney means no potassium excretion and no acid excretion. Acidosis pushes still more potassium out of cells. The rising extracellular potassium narrows the gap between resting and threshold potential, and the ECG reports that as peaked T waves, then lost P waves, then a wide QRS, then a sine wave.

The treatment order follows directly from what each drug does. **Calcium protects** the membrane in 1-3 minutes and lowers nothing. **Insulin and albuterol move** potassium into cells for 4-6 hours and remove nothing. **Only dialysis and diuresis remove.** Steps one and two are a bridge, and if you never build the far end of that bridge, the potassium comes back out.

Two habits to carry: get the ECG before the laboratory calls, and keep everything off the fistula arm.

scenarios.title: Reasoning it out: vomiting, deep breathing, glucose 480
scenarios.intro:
A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has been vomiting for two days with a viral illness and stopped taking her insulin because she "wasn't eating anything." A fingerstick glucose reads 480 mg/dL. She is awake, answering questions, and breathing deeply and rapidly without appearing to struggle.

Work the mechanism at every step. The management follows from it.

steps.prompt:
Her respirations are deep and regular at 32 per minute. Her lungs are clear, her oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and her breath has a faintly sweet, solvent-like smell.

What is the breathing telling you?

choices.text: Kussmaul respirations: the lungs are compensating for a metabolic acidosis by blowing off carbon dioxide
choices.feedback: Correct. Deep and fast with clear lungs and a normal saturation is respiratory compensation, not a lung problem. The fruity smell is acetone, a ketone volatile enough to leave through the breath. This is the body defending its pH.

choices.text: Primary respiratory alkalosis from anxiety and pain
choices.feedback: Tempting because the rate is high, but anxious hyperventilation is usually shallow and irregular with tingling fingers. Kussmaul breathing is deep, regular and effortless, and it appears in a patient with an obvious metabolic reason for it.

choices.text: Early pneumonia driving the respiratory rate
choices.feedback: Clear lungs, a saturation of 99% and no fever argue against it, though infection is a common trigger for DKA and deserves a look. The breathing pattern itself is compensation, not the disease.

choices.text: Impending respiratory failure requiring immediate intubation
choices.feedback: Harmful. That respiratory drive is the only thing holding her pH up. Intubating her and ventilating at a normal rate drops her minute ventilation, her carbon dioxide climbs, and her pH crashes. Avoid intubation in DKA unless there is no alternative.

steps.prompt:
Laboratory results: glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, anion gap 28, sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, large serum ketones.

What is the first therapeutic move?

choices.text: Start isotonic crystalloid at roughly 15-20 mL/kg over the first hour
choices.feedback: Correct. She has been running an osmotic diuresis for two days and is likely 4-6 L down, which is 5-10% of body weight. Volume alone lowers glucose, improves renal perfusion so she can excrete ketoacids, and restores the blood pressure that everything else depends on.

choices.text: Start the insulin infusion immediately, before any fluid
choices.feedback: Harmful ordering. Insulin drives glucose and water back into cells, which can drop an already low intravascular volume further, and it drives potassium in before you know where the potassium really stands. Fluids first, and check the potassium before insulin.

choices.text: Give sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH of 7.12
choices.feedback: Not indicated. Bicarbonate is generally reserved for a pH below 6.9. Given earlier it worsens intracellular acidosis, drops potassium further and delays ketone clearance. The acidosis resolves when the ketone production stops.

choices.text: Give an antiemetic and observe for a few hours
choices.feedback: An antiemetic is reasonable as an adjunct, but observation alone in a patient with a pH of 7.12 and an anion gap of 28 is dangerous. This is an active metabolic emergency that gets worse without intervention.

steps.prompt:
Fluids are running. Your attending points at the potassium of 5.1 mEq/L and asks: "Is that number reassuring?"

What is the correct answer?

choices.text: No. Acidosis has shifted potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis has been dumping it in urine, so total body potassium is depleted despite a serum level in range
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Hydrogen moves into cells to be buffered and potassium moves out to keep charge balance, inflating the serum value. Meanwhile she has been urinating potassium for two days. The serum number is a snapshot of distribution, not of stores.

choices.text: No, it is falsely elevated because the sample hemolyzed
choices.feedback: Hemolysis does falsely raise potassium and is worth ruling out on any surprising value, but it is not what is happening here. The mechanism is a transcellular shift driven by acidosis on top of real total-body depletion.

choices.text: Yes. 5.1 mEq/L is within the normal range, so potassium needs no further thought
choices.feedback: This is the classic DKA trap and it is how patients are harmed. A normal-looking potassium in DKA is a warning, not reassurance. It will fall the moment insulin starts.

choices.text: No, it is dangerously high and she should receive calcium gluconate
choices.feedback: Overcorrection in the wrong direction. 5.1 is barely above the reference range with no ECG changes, and the real risk in DKA is hypokalemia during treatment, not hyperkalemic arrest. Calcium has no role here.

steps.prompt:
The insulin infusion has been running at 0.1 units/kg/hr for two hours. Repeat labs: glucose 288 mg/dL, potassium 3.6 mEq/L, anion gap 20, pH 7.24.

What now?

choices.text: Add potassium to the intravenous fluids and continue the insulin infusion
choices.feedback: Correct. Between 3.3 and 5.2 mEq/L, potassium is replaced alongside the insulin, typically 20-30 mEq per liter of fluid, with the level rechecked every 2-4 hours. The gap is closing, which means the insulin is doing its job on the acidosis.

choices.text: Stop the insulin infusion entirely to protect the potassium
choices.feedback: Overreaction. The insulin is what is clearing the ketones, and stopping it re-opens the anion gap. You would only hold insulin below 3.3 mEq/L, and even then only until potassium is replaced.

choices.text: Do nothing; 3.6 mEq/L is within the normal range
choices.feedback: The trend matters more than the value. She dropped 1.5 mEq/L in two hours on an empty tank, and the insulin is still running. Waiting until she is frankly hypokalemic means treating an arrhythmia instead of preventing one.

choices.text: Increase the insulin rate to clear the ketones faster
choices.feedback: Harmful. A higher rate does not close the gap faster in any meaningful way, and it accelerates the potassium and glucose fall. The standard 0.1 units/kg/hr exists precisely because faster is not safer.

steps.prompt:
Four hours in: glucose 196 mg/dL, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, anion gap 17, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, pH 7.29. She has stopped vomiting and her respiratory rate is 22.

What is the right next step?

choices.text: Add dextrose to the intravenous fluids and keep the insulin infusion running until the anion gap closes
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the concept that separates people who understand DKA from people who memorized it. The insulin is treating the ketoacidosis, not the glucose. Dextrose goes in so you can keep the insulin running without causing hypoglycemia.

choices.text: Stop the insulin infusion now that the glucose is nearly normal
choices.feedback: A common and costly error. With a gap of 17 she is still making ketones. Stopping insulin lets lipolysis restart and the gap reopens, and she is back where she started a few hours later.

choices.text: Switch to subcutaneous insulin immediately and stop the drip
choices.feedback: Too early, and the overlap matters. The transition happens once the gap has closed and she is eating, and the subcutaneous dose is given 1-2 hours before the drip is stopped, because intravenous insulin disappears within minutes.

choices.text: Continue hourly glucose checks and recheck electrolytes and the gap every 2-4 hours
choices.feedback: Correct monitoring and it should be happening, but it is not the intervention the question is asking for. Monitoring tells you what is happening; the dextrose is what lets treatment continue.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **in DKA you are treating an acid problem, not a sugar problem.** The glucose is the most visible number and the least important one.

The mechanism chain, forward: no insulin, so glucose cannot enter cells; cells starve and fat is mobilized; the liver turns fatty acids into ketoacids; pH falls and the anion gap opens; the lungs compensate with Kussmaul respirations and acetone leaves on the breath; glucose above about 180 mg/dL spills into urine and drags water and electrolytes out for days.

The potassium trap is the exam favorite and the bedside danger. Acidosis pushes potassium out of cells and inflates the serum value while the kidney has been dumping potassium the whole time. **A normal potassium in DKA means a depleted patient**, and insulin will unmask it within an hour. Hold insulin below `3.3 mEq/L`, replace alongside between `3.3` and `5.2`.

Finally, remember what each piece treats: fluids treat the volume deficit, insulin treats the ketoacidosis, dextrose exists so the insulin can keep running, and bicarbonate stays in the drawer unless the pH is below 6.9. The endpoint is a closed anion gap, not a normal glucose.
